---
title: "Metrics to measure correlation of metaprograms"
author: "Ally Hawkins"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_notebook
---

This notebook looks at the distributions of three different correlation-based metrics and attempts to define some lenient cutoffs for what's considered a good or bad result. 

Note that some of this setup code and box plot code comes from the original exploratory notebook in `03-metaprogram-comparison.Rmd`. 
I am repeating it here to have everything related to correlation metrics in the same place. 


```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# Set default ggplot theme
theme_set(
  theme_bw()
)
```

## Functions

```{r}
# a little helper function to look at histogram and density plots for a single metric
plot_distribution <- function(df, column){
  
  hist <- ggplot(df, aes(x = !!sym(column))) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "grey90", color = "black") 
  
  density <- ggplot(df, aes(x = !!sym(column))) +
    geom_density(fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5)
  
  hist / density
}
```


## Set Up 


```{r}
# metaprograms results directory
results_dir <- here::here("ews-nf-out", "metaprograms")

# params we are looking at in this particular notebook 
# use these to construct the file paths 
n_metaprograms <- seq(6, 15, 1)

# directories with metaprogram results 
# one directory per n_metaprogram
metaprogram_output_dirs <- file.path(
  results_dir, 
  glue::glue("metaprograms-{n_metaprograms}_cnmf-5-10-15_filtered")
) |> 
  # set names here so we can use them to read in the score files
  purrr::set_names(sprintf("k_%02d", n_metaprograms))


# path to files with each of the metrics
metrics_files <- file.path(metaprogram_output_dirs, "metaprograms-metrics.rds") |> 
  # file.path doesn't keep the names so set them again 
  purrr::set_names(sprintf("k_%02d", n_metaprograms))
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
# get the metrics files 
mp_metrics_list <- metrics_files |> 
  purrr::map(readr::read_rds)

# create dataframe with one row per metaprogram/n_metaprogram (k) combination 
# each column is a metric for that metaprograms
mp_metrics_df <- mp_metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(metrics_list) metrics_list$mp_metrics_df) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")
```

```{r}
# path to files with the scores for each of the outputs
# each sample with each k/n_metaprograms has it's own file
# so go through each of the directories and find the score files to join together
# note that trying to read in all the files and then join at once caused R to crash 
scores_df <- metaprogram_output_dirs |> 
  purrr::map(\(dir){
    
    files <- list.files(
      path = dir,
      pattern = "_metaprogram_scores.tsv",
      recursive = TRUE,
      full.names = TRUE
    )
    
    # read in dataframe with metaprogra(e.g., MP01), barcodes, mp_score, and unique_id
    # one row per cell per mp
    files |> 
      purrr::map(\(f) {
        readr::read_tsv(
          f, 
          col_types = 
            list(metaprogram = "c", barcodes = "c", mp_score = "n", unique_id = "c")
        )
      })|> 
      dplyr::bind_rows()
    
  }) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")
```


## Max correlation - genes 

First we'll look at the correlation of metaprograms at the gene level. 
This is calculated by computing the pairwise correlation of all genes across all metaprograms. 

```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of metaprogram gene weights"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed")
```

Let's look at the distribution of all points together regardless of the value of k to see if we can identify any obvious inflection points. 

```{r}
hist <- ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = max_correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "grey90", color = "black") 

density <- ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = max_correlation)) +
  geom_density(fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5)

hist / density
```
There doesn't seem to be a single inflection point or place that obviously has outliers. 
Looking at the density plot it almost looks bimodal with half the MPs having > 0.2 correlation. 
I don't think we want to use that as a cutoff though because correlation between 0.2 and 0.4 still seem reasonable and not too high. 
I also don't want to say half our MPs are bad, which is what would happen if we use that cutoff. 


What if we just get the mean of the max correlation and look for the value of k that has the minimum value? 

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    mean_correlation = mean(max_correlation)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(mean_correlation)
```

Interestingly k=7 is at the top, which was one of the "top" scoring metaprogram when looking at some of the sample diversity metrics. 

## Max correlation - cells 

Next we'll look at the correlation of scores for the top 200 genes across all cells. 
To do this we first get a cell by metaprogram matrix where the values correspond to the scores for that metaprogram in that cell. 
Then we calculate the pairwise correlation. 


```{r}
# split by value of k
split_scores_list <- split(scores_df, scores_df$n_metaprograms)

# separately calculate the correlation of metaprograms for each value of k 
# then get the max for each metaprogram and combine back into a single df for plotting
score_correlation_df <- split_scores_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(df){
    mtx <- df |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(
        names_from = "metaprogram",
        values_from = "mp_score"
      ) |> 
      dplyr::mutate(cell_id = glue::glue("{unique_id}_{barcodes}")) |> 
      dplyr::select(-c(n_metaprograms, unique_id, barcodes)) |> 
      tibble::column_to_rownames("cell_id") |> 
      as.matrix()
    
    # correlation of scores for each cell 
    cor_mtx <- cor(mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    
    # get the non-self max
    diag(cor_mtx) <- 0
    max_cor_df <- data.frame(
      metaprogram = rownames(cor_mtx),
      max_correlation_cells = MatrixGenerics::rowMaxs(cor_mtx)
    )
    
  }) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")
```


```{r}
ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of cell scores"
  ) 
```

Again, we'll look at the distribution of all points together. 

```{r}
hist <- ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "grey90", color = "black") 

density <- ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_density(fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5)

hist / density
```

Notably, this correlation range is much wider and we see a spike in correlations around 0.6.
We might be able to say that anything above 0.8 is an outlier and is considered "high" correlation given the small tail there? 

Alternatively, we could try and define outliers as those with a zscore > 2. 

```{r}
score_correlation_df <- score_correlation_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(correlation_zscore = scale(max_correlation_cells),
                correlation_is_outlier = correlation_zscore > 2)

ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = correlation_is_outlier)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of cell scores"
  ) 
```

Hmm it doesn't look like there are any outliers. 

```{r}
summary(score_correlation_df$correlation_zscore)
```

Indeed if you look at the range of the z-scores the highest zscore is 1.5. 
So maybe we should just the use the > 0.8 cutoff. 

Similar to the gene correlation, we can rank based on the mean correlation and look for the value of k with the minimum correlation values. 

```{r}
score_correlation_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    mean_correlation_cells = mean(max_correlation_cells)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(mean_correlation_cells)
```

Looks like k=7 is at the top again. 

## Difference in medians

Finally, we'll look at the difference in medians between the distribution of correlation of spectra within a given metaprogram and between metaprograms. 
Here we want to maximize the value. 


```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Difference in medians of correlation \n within - between metaprograms"
  )
```

```{r}
plot_distribution(mp_metrics_df, "median_difference")
```

Here it looks like the majority of values are centered around 0.3 and we have a little bump in the beginning of what may be outliers. 
Let's formally look for some outliers by using a zscore again. 
We'll call anything with z < -2 an outlier. 

```{r}
mp_metrics_df <- mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::mutate(median_diff_zscore = scale(median_difference),
                median_diff_is_outlier = median_diff_zscore < -2)

ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = median_diff_is_outlier)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of cell scores"
  ) 
```

As predicted, that bottom point in every value of k is considered an outlier. 

Alternatively, we can take the same approach of calculating the mean value and finding the value of k with the maximum. 

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    mean_difference = mean(median_difference)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(mean_difference))
```

Interestingly, this metric seems to be almost dependent on the value of k. 
It looks like around the k=12/11/13 area there's a mixup but if we used this metric alone, k=15 would be the winner. 

Since we already know that single bad program is going to get thrown out across the board, let's look at the values of the other metrics for that outlier. 

```{r}
all_stats_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::left_join(score_correlation_df, by = c("n_metaprograms", "metaprogram"))

all_stats_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(median_diff_is_outlier) |> 
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, metaprogram, max_correlation, max_correlation_cells, median_difference)
```

Interestingly, the values for the other metrics for that program are below the thresholds we had picked. 
Maybe correlation between metaprograoms isn't the best metric for choosing "good" metaprograms since inherently they should be different from each other. 
It's possible that we might want to drop the gene and cell correlation and only look at the difference of medians. 

## Combining metrics 

Finally, I'll look at the combination of all of them to see if we can create a single correlation metric that might be useful moving forward. 
For this I'll calculate the proportion of metaprograms that pass each of our thresholds and then take the mean proportion of those numbers.

```{r}
all_stats_df |> 
  # first add columns to indicate if the MP passed each threshold
  dplyr::mutate(
    passing_gene_correlation = max_correlation < 0.3,
    passing_cell_correlation = max_correlation_cells < 0.8,
    passing_median_diff = median_diff_zscore > -2
  ) |> 
  # now calculate the proportion for each one individually and then get the mean
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_mps = length(unique(metaprogram)),
    proportion_passing_gene_correlation = sum(passing_gene_correlation)/num_mps,
    proportion_passing_cell_correlation = sum(passing_cell_correlation)/num_mps,
    proportion_passing_median_diff = sum(passing_median_diff)/num_mps,
    mean_all_passing = mean(c(proportion_passing_gene_correlation,
                              proportion_passing_cell_correlation,
                              proportion_passing_median_diff))
  ) |> 
  dplyr::select(-num_mps) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(mean_all_passing))
```

If we take the mean proportion of all MPs passing each of the correlation related metrics and then rank them we again see k=7 and k=11 near the top, which is consistent with the sample diversity metrics. 

## Concluding thoughts

* It looks like we could set lenient cutoffs for the gene and cell correlation metrics and then use an outlier based approach for the median difference (or also set a lenient cutoff). 
We could then combine these to create a single "correlation" metric by looking at the proportion of MPs that pass each of these metrics. 
* Or we could keep them separate and only consider combining them when we look at all metrics together. 
* Another approach is to be even less stringent and identify outliers for all the correlation metrics which would result in all MPs passing the gene and cell correlations and all but one MP passing the median difference threshold. 
For this particular subset, there's no differences between the values of k, but maybe that's okay for these. 
* Perhaps we should drop the gene and cell correlations all together and just use the median difference?
